claims.claim: Shortcuts vs mirroring guidance, and mirroring replicates when the source stores data in a proprietary format.
Replication compute is free and does not consume capacity; mirroring storage is free at 1 TB per CU; MySQL, Dremio and SharePoint List sources are in preview; BigQuery is GA.

Azure SQL Database mirroring: 1,000 tables maximum, datetime2(7)/datetimeoffset(7)/time(7) primary keys unsupported, tables without primary keys supported since April 2025 but not added automatically.

concept_html:
Mirroring brings an external database into Fabric as a unit. For sources that store data in their own formats, such as Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, Azure Cosmos DB, Snowflake or Google BigQuery, Fabric continuously replicates the chosen tables into OneLake as Delta tables, in near real time. You get a mirrored database item and a SQL analytics endpoint over it, read-only, like a lakehouse's.

Shortcut or mirroring? Microsoft Learn's rule:

  • Shortcut when you want specific data, already in an open format, in your OneLake view without copying it.
  • Mirroring when you want an external database or catalog, and the data behind it, in Fabric as a unit. It replicates when the source uses a proprietary format.

Cost. For database mirroring and open mirroring, the background compute that replicates data does not consume capacity. Mirrored storage is free up to 1 TB per capacity unit: an F64 includes 64 TB of mirroring storage. Queries on the mirrored data (Spark, SQL, Power BI) use capacity as usual.

Limits come per source. For Azure SQL Database, checked September 2026:

  • at most 1,000 mirrored tables per database,
  • tables whose primary key uses datetime2(7), datetimeoffset(7) or time(7) cannot be mirrored,
  • since April 2025 tables without a primary key can be mirrored, but existing ones are not added automatically, even with "Automatically mirror future tables" turned on.

Status varies too. Most sources are generally available. Some, such as Azure Database for MySQL, Dremio and SharePoint List, were in preview in September 2026. Check the mirroring overview page before you build on a source.

After you set up a mirror, compare row counts per table between source and mirror (lesson A6-L3). The limits above fail quietly: an ineligible table is simply not there.

lines: -- Run in the source database: tables and row counts
SELECT s.name AS schema_name, t.name AS table_name, SUM(p.rows) AS source_rows
FROM sys.tables AS t
JOIN sys.schemas AS s ON s.schema_id = t.schema_id
JOIN sys.partitions AS p ON p.object_id = t.object_id AND p.index_id IN (0, 1)
GROUP BY s.name, t.name;
-- Run on the mirror's SQL analytics endpoint: which tables arrived
SELECT TABLE_SCHEMA, TABLE_NAME
FROM INFORMATION_SCHEMA.TABLES
WHERE TABLE_TYPE = 'BASE TABLE';

exercises.prompt: Write `missing_from_mirror(source: dict[str, int], mirror: dict[str, int]) -> list[str]` for a reconciliation job. Both map `schema.table` to a row count. Return, sorted, the tables that are absent from the mirror, or whose mirror count differs from the source count.
exercises.prompt_html: Write missing_from_mirror(source: dict[str, int], mirror: dict[str, int]) -> list[str] for a reconciliation job. Both map schema.table to a row count. Return, sorted, the tables that are absent from the mirror, or whose mirror count differs from the source count.
exercises.solution:
def missing_from_mirror(source: dict[str, int], mirror: dict[str, int]) -> list[str]:
    """Source tables that are absent from the mirror or differ in row count.

    Args:
        source: schema.table to row count in the source database.
        mirror: schema.table to row count on the mirror's endpoint.

    Returns:
        Sorted table names that need attention.
    """
    return sorted(t for t, n in source.items() if mirror.get(t) != n)

title: Mirroring operational databases into OneLake
why_html: A team mirrored an Azure SQL order database and built a dashboard on it. Weeks later, finance noticed that returns were missing. The returns table's primary key included a datetime2(7) column, so it had never been mirrored. Nothing errored. A per-table row-count check between source and mirror on the first day would have listed it as absent.
